What do these score bands mean?

These quartiles describe MyTriRanking overall scores among all British women uniquely matched to either saved PTO or OpenRank list. Each athlete counts once; ambiguous names are excluded. The group stays the same when you zoom the chart or change the prediction model.

The shaded band contains the middle half of this group’s score distribution, between the 25th and 75th percentiles. The median divides it in half. Higher scores are better. Percentiles are interpolated between ordered scores, so boundaries need not equal an athlete’s exact score.

These are descriptive benchmarks for this British comparison group. They are neither professional eligibility thresholds nor worldwide professional ranking bands.

These are the closest uniquely matched athletes above and below your overall score in the supplied British list. The gaps are observed MyTriRanking points, not predictions of race time or pro rank.

How to read the colours: burgundy means a unique name match in the saved PTO or OpenRank lists. Pale aqua means no match, not confirmed amateur status. Pink diamonds mark duplicate names we cannot safely assign. You are highlighted separately in crimson. These are the supplied British rankings, not the worldwide MyTriRanking field; this section is independent of the model controls above.

How this simulator works

A target UK rank uses the overall score at that position in the saved British women’s middle-distance list. A score target is compared with that list, excluding your existing entry; equal scores share a position here. This is a comparison with a fixed field, not an official tie-break calculation or a future ranking forecast.

Every saved bootstrap line is evaluated at the new score. The prediction interval also keeps that draw’s sampled between-athlete variation. Both intervals are recalculated at the target; they are not shifted copies of your current interval.

The ranking system, comparison approach, athlete group, method and scoring finishes follow the settings above. This explorer always uses overall-score models, even if the other charts use best-race scores. For PTO season scenarios, the selected number of comparable scoring finishes is still assumed. Other athletes’ scores are held fixed.

These are provisional model comparisons, not evidence that reaching a UK target would cause that world rank. Race times and bike power are not converted into scores in this first version. Your recorded results and saved history stay unchanged.

What happens when we update the data?

We save the new rankings and matching PTO scoring evidence as a new dated snapshot, run the same analysis, then update this page. Earlier snapshots keep their original data and model results.

The newest date becomes the default view. You can still select any previous date, and the history plot and comparison cards fill in automatically. The date in the page address also lets you return to a particular saved download.

Nothing refreshes automatically in the background. The dates here mean data downloaded on that day, not that every ranking was calculated that day. See “Data coverage and sources” for the selected snapshot’s available ranking dates.

Two intervals, two different questions

Read the wider prediction interval when thinking about your own possible result.

How certain is the fitted relationship?

How much the model’s fitted mean changes when we resample the comparison athletes.

How much might an individual vary?

Adds the variation seen between athletes. This is the more relevant spread for an individual estimate.

What sits outside both intervals?

  • Age-group versus pro race conditions
  • Different courses and distances
  • Who enters the ranked comparison group
  • Whether the season assumptions hold

These are exploratory model-based intervals. They are not a 95% probability statement about your true world rank.

The provisional world estimate

How the statistics are calculated

for definitions and examples. This dashboard uses estimation methods and model checks; it does not report significance tests or p-values.

  1. Match athlete names after removing punctuation and accents and ignoring case. Exclude ambiguous duplicate names from modelling. Preserve the source ranking tables unchanged.
  2. For PTO race performance, use the mean of positive results in each athlete’s displayed scoring breakdown. Zero-point rows remain in the evidence. This estimates a successful-scoring-finishes scenario, rather than the risk of DNFs or an incomplete season.
  3. Fit either ordinary least squares or Huber robust regression. Robust regression reduces the influence of large residuals; it does not resolve differences between the ranking systems.
  4. For each configuration, resample athletes with replacement 1,000 times and refit the model. The 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles give an exploratory 95% bootstrap confidence interval for the fitted mean.
  5. For the prediction distribution, add a sampled, centred, leverage-adjusted residual to each bootstrap fitted value. This adds between-athlete scatter. It assumes this scatter is applicable at my score and does not shrink by the square root of four races.
  6. For PTO performance, multiply each race-score draw by the chosen scoring-finish count, divide by four, then count how many entries in the saved PTO table have more points. Other athletes stay fixed. Ties require official rules.
  7. For published-rank models, fit rank directly and round the draws to whole positions. Display ranks below 1 at 1 and beyond the last listed athlete as “N+”. Boundary mass is reported. This is a snapshot comparison, not a full-season ability estimate.
  8. The confidence band is for the fitted mean only. Cohort and method selection are not included in any one interval. Compare the alternatives to see that sensitivity. Intervals are exploratory, rely on exchangeability and residual assumptions, and are not validated coverage guarantees.

MyTriRanking “overall” and “best” use the matching score column for every athlete. The nearby group always means overall MyTriRanking score below 900. The complete-results group means four positive displayed PTO scores. Leave-one-out error refits without each athlete in turn.

Each configuration uses a fixed random seed for reproducibility. Confidence and prediction intervals use the percentile method. The distribution bars show the share of simulated draws in a rank bin, not an empirically validated probability of my real rank.

R documentation: confidence and prediction intervals · Huber robust regression in MASS

Data coverage and sources

  • MyTriRanking:
  • PTO World Rankings:
  • ProTriNews OpenRank:
  • PTO methodology · OpenRank methodology. Their scores are not interchangeable.

There is no claim here to an official rank or pro eligibility. The target is a position within the selected ranking’s current listed field, not all female triathletes worldwide. Same-course, same-day comparisons would strengthen the analysis. A year-end comparison requires matching historical performance data and scoring rules.

Re-knit this dashboard in RStudio

Open ranking-dashboard.Rmd and click Knit to rebuild the page from every saved snapshot. Rebuilding the page preserves historical estimates. Keep the source files and data/snapshots folder together.

For a new download, follow UPDATE-INSTRUCTIONS.txt beside the Rmd. The update process checks matching download dates and PTO scoring evidence, saves a new dated bundle, and rebuilds the HTML for review and publication. It refuses to overwrite an existing date.

All supported model results are embedded in the HTML, so the date selector and other controls work offline. Packages: rmarkdown, knitr, MASS and jsonlite.
